analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for the President or Vice President to sell nonpublic government information for profit.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill has six Democratic cosponsors and no further action since arrival.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it a federal crime for the President or Vice President — and any business they control or own at least 5 percent of — to sell or exchange nonpublic government information for financial gain. It also makes it a crime for anyone else to buy or trade on that information. Penalties include up to 5 years in prison, fines up to double the value of the deal, forfeiture of profits, and a civil lawsuit by the Attorney General to claw back proceeds. Introduced in August 2026, it was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: The public. The bill targets the scenario where the person with the most access to secret government information can sell or trade on it. It applies to the President and Vice President directly, and to any company they control or own at least 5 percent of, so profits routed through a family business would still be reachable. It closes the loop by criminalizing the buyers: any person who acquires such information for financial benefit is liable too.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, not the Oval Office

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new criminal offense barring the President or Vice President, and any entity they control or own 5 percent or more of, from selling or exchanging nonpublic information gained through their official position for financial benefit, punishable by up to 5 years in prison and a fine of up to double the transaction's value.

Criminalizes the other side of the deal: any person who acquires, purchases, sells, or exchanges such nonpublic information for financial benefit commits an offense, with a fine of up to double the transaction's value and forfeiture of any proceeds.

Lets the Attorney General sue to claw back profits without waiting for a criminal conviction, using a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, with a civil penalty up to the greater of $250,000 or triple the gain, and a 6-year clock that pauses while the person holds the office of President or Vice President.
Requires the Office of Government Ethics to refer credible evidence of violations to the Attorney General and to notify the House and Senate Judiciary Committees of each referral.

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, and their affiliated business entities, who could no longer monetize nonpublic information gained in office, plus any outside buyer or counterparty who would have paid for that information.
analysis.who_pays_short: The President, VP, and their businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only the President and Vice President. It does not reach members of Congress, federal judges, or other senior officials who trade on nonpublic information, so it addresses a slice of the problem rather than the whole.

Enforcement depends entirely on the Attorney General. A president's own Justice Department could decline to prosecute or sue, which is why the bill adds an OGE referral duty and a tolling rule but still leaves the trigger in the administration's hands.

The definition of nonpublic information is broad — it includes statements or communications not made available to the general public on equal terms — which could invite vagueness challenges and complicate routine, selective official communications.

The civil case uses a lower standard of proof than a criminal trial and the statute of limitations pauses during the term, meaning an ex-president could face a lawsuit years after leaving office over conduct that was never formally resolved while in office.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rule is narrow and well-aimed: the two officials with the greatest access to market-moving secrets could no longer sell them, and the people who would buy them become liable too. Its real weaknesses are scope and enforcement — it leaves every other federal official untouched, and it counts on a Justice Department that answers to the president to police the president. The tolling provision partially offsets the enforcement problem by keeping the door open after the term ends.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2026 and sent straight to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrea Salinas introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, joined by Reps. Mfume, Bynum, and Norton as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action has been taken.
Six House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has.

The bill would be added to title 18 of the U.S. Code as a new offense, 'Misuse of nonpublic information,' applying to the President and Vice President and entities they control or own at least 5 percent of.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill sitting untouched in committee, sitting officials and their business affiliates remain free to transact on nonpublic information without this penalty, and would-be buyers face no new exposure. The public does not get the protection the bill would provide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials free to trade on secrets

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on its introduction day and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a House Democrat and no Republican has signed on; the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee has taken no action since the referral.

industries.industry: Business entities owned or controlled by the President or Vice President
industries.note: The bill's 'covered entity' definition captures any firm such an official controls or owns at least 5 percent of, so a family business could no longer sell or exchange nonpublic information gained through the office. Their interest in defeating the bill runs against the public's interest in an honest executive branch.

industries.industry: Traders and investors who would buy nonpublic government information
industries.note: Anyone who acquires such information for financial benefit commits an offense, with fines up to double the transaction's value and forfeiture of proceeds. Their profit came from information the public never had, so their loss is the public's gain.

analysis.trajectory: The House session ends January 3, 2027. With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action since the August referral, the realistic path is that the bill expires without a vote, and a successor version would have to be reintroduced in the next Congress.
